figures.caption: From task-specific webpage optimization to interactive HTML capability catalysis. WebCatalyst improves fidelity in interaction experience, reward signals, and credit assignment through a Game-Level GUI Assessor, Visual Anchor, and Action-Trace Credit.
figures.headline: The framework targets three fidelity gaps: interaction experience, reward signal, and credit assignment.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Overview of WebCatalyst’s browser-interaction RL framework. Training requests come from Reddit, and sampled HTML artifacts are execute in Playwright. The game-level GUI Assessor combines sustained interaction with hierarchical judgment for page-level rewards. Visual Anchor penalizes visual degradation relative to reference screenshots, while Action-Trace Credit maps successful actions’ runtime call paths to generated tokens and redistributes fine-grained advantages. GRPO optimizes the generation policy using the calibrated rewards and token-level advantages. Gameplay examples illustrate functionality and visual quality before and after training.
figures.headline: The training loop feeds GUI Assessor rewards, a Visual Anchor penalty, and token-level credit into GRPO updates.
citing_sentences: To move beyond task-specific webpage training toward catalyzing transferable capabilities for more demanding interactive HTML generation, we integrate interactive execution, reference calibration, and runtime-grounded credit assignment in one training framework (Figure 2).

abstract: Generating HTML from natural-language specifications is an important application of code large language models (LLMs). Despite producing renderable pages, current models often fail to ensure functionality and visual quality during actual interaction. Existing methods typically target task-specific webpage supervision, leaving demanding interactive artifact optimization underexplored. Using mini-games as a challenging testbed, we expose limitations in interaction experience, reward signal, and credit assignment fidelity that are obscured by shallow webpage interactions. We introduce WebCatalyst, a browser-interaction reinforcement learning framework with three complementary components: a game-level GUI assessor for sustained interaction and evaluation, Visual Anchor for mitigating VLM reward hacking, and Action-Trace Credit for grounding token-level credit assignment in runtime execution traces. Trained on fewer than 1K requests, predominantly for games, WebCatalyst raises the Cookie-Bench Mini Games score from 68.8 to 75.3 and also the WebGen-Bench accuracy from 48.8 to 56.9 on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, outperforming Claude Opus 4.7 in average rank across evaluated metrics. Further analysis shows that Visual Anchor prevents aesthetic degradation, while runtime-grounded credit assignment accelerates functional improvement. Together, our results show that improving feedback fidelity is the key to substantially advancing interactive HTML generation.

sections.body: The introduction argues that a page can render yet fail once a user interacts with it, so usability depends on behavior during interaction. Recent reinforcement-learning methods for webpages use task-specific supervision. The paper uses mini-games as a harder testbed and identifies three gaps: interaction experience, reward signal, and credit assignment. WebCatalyst addresses them with a Game-Level GUI Assessor, Visual Anchor against VLM reward hacking, and Action-Trace Credit. With fewer than 1K training requests, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B rises from 68.8 to 75.3 on Cookie-Bench Mini Games and from 48.8 to 56.9 on WebGen-Bench.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Interactive HTML quality depends on behavior during use, so the paper uses mini-games as a harder test.

sections.body: Related work covers three areas. Assessment work uses GUI agents and interaction-aware benchmarks, but these mainly serve benchmarking or inference-time refinement rather than training feedback. Training work for HTML generation uses supervised screenshot-code pairs, browser-guided data, and reinforcement-learning methods that mostly target webpage generation with task-specific evaluation protocols. Code credit-assignment work localizes feedback with learned reward models, compiler-reported errors, execution coverage, or a single related code span. The paper states that Action-Trace Credit traces each successful GUI action to its runtime code path, and that its focus is supervision fidelity in sustained HTML interaction.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior work evaluates interactive HTML or trains on webpages, but rarely uses interactive assessors as reinforcement-learning feedback.

sections.body: Each requirement yields a group of sampled responses that are rendered as pages. The GUI Assessor runs a ReAct-style Execution Agent over a browser state machine, choosing from click, hover, mouseMove, press, combo, type, wait, and terminate. A step-level judge scores each transition, and a meta-level judge aggregates them into a page score. Visual Anchor compares screenshots with reference screenshots and estimates a one-sided degradation $D_i$. The calibrated reward is $r_{i}=\frac{R_{i}^{\mathrm{GUI}}-D_{i}}{100}$. Action-Trace Credit captures JavaScript call stacks for successful actions, maps executed code spans to generated tokens, and scales token advantages by call depth, with decay $\gamma$ and modulation strength $\beta$ below 1. The policy is updated with GRPO.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: WebCatalyst combines an interactive assessor, a reference-based visual penalty, and call-trace token credit in one policy update.

sections.body: The benchmarks are WebGen-Bench, with 101 requests and 647 test cases, and 156 deduplicated Cookie-Bench Mini Games requests, where UI-TARS drives the browser. Table 1 gives the base Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 48.8 WebGen-Bench accuracy and 68.8 Mini Games total, versus 56.9 and 75.3 for WebCatalyst, with Avg. Rank 14.0 versus 4.0. In the training analysis, GUI-only feedback improves functionality while Mini Games aesthetics deteriorate. A GPT-5.5 Anchor remains stable across training, while a Self Anchor deteriorates in later steps. Action-Trace Credit reduces training steps to reach a comparable EMA critic score by approximately 1.84×. Table 3 shows that after three refinement rounds WebCatalyst reaches Total 76.9, above the backbone's best of 75.2.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: WebCatalyst raises WebGen-Bench accuracy from 48.8 to 56.9 and reaches average rank 4.0 against 4.7 for Claude-Opus-4.7.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the contribution: a unified browser-interaction reinforcement-learning framework that improves supervision fidelity across interaction experience, reward signals, and credit assignment. Trained on fewer than 1K requests, primarily mini-games, WebCatalyst substantially improves mini-game generation, and its gains transfer to conventional webpage tasks. The authors argue that high-fidelity feedback is the key to moving beyond task-specific webpage optimization toward more capable interactive HTML generation. The section introduces no new experiments.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Fewer than 1K requests, mostly mini-games, improved mini-game generation and transferred to webpage tasks.

sections.body: The limitations fall into three points. The work covers direct generation only and does not optimize planning, iterative debugging, or tool-use pipelines. Reinforcement learning activates capabilities already present in the base model and complements rather than replaces SFT, so its effect depends on those prior capabilities. Training used game prompts, and the effects of task mixtures and data composition are left to future work. The section also notes misuse risks, including deceptive interfaces, phishing websites, and malicious client-side behaviors, and calls for safeguards at deployment.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Limits include direct generation only, dependence on base-model capabilities, and training on game prompts.

sections.body: Appendix A details the GUI Assessor: a fresh Chromium context at a fixed 1440×900 viewport, an Execution Agent limited to a grounded action interface, a queued step-level judge with weighted component scores, and a meta-level judge whose score is capped by a usability rubric. It also describes tracing JavaScript call stacks through the Chrome DevTools Protocol and mapping them to tokens. A judge selection study with more than 70 artifacts reports Pearson correlations with human ratings of 0.613 for Qwen3.6-27B, 0.838 for Qwen3.8-27B, and 0.812 for GPT-5.6 Terra, and 0.309 for Src-Rubric. Qwen3.8-27B reaches a Mini Games Total of 72.4, against 75.3 for GPT-5.6 Terra. The section ends with the prompts used for generation and assessment.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix covers the GUI Assessor pipeline, trace-to-token mapping, judge selection, prompts, and comparison figures.
